_about: Week 5 support videos (Stuck? buttons). Links are supplied and checked by Dr. Rennie; assemble_w05.py reads this file. V is keyed by a short id; SUP maps an exact step title to [button label, video id, what to listen for]. A V entry may carry s, the channel name, when the video is not from Khan Academy; the button then names that channel.

wx.n: How reflexes work: the reflex arc, monosynaptic and polysynaptic reflexes

Every reflex follows one path: What are the parts of a reflex arc?
Listen for the five parts in order: receptor, sensory neuron, integrating center, motor neuron, effector.
Where the signal goes: What are the parts of a reflex arc?
Listen for where the sensory neuron enters the cord and where the motor neuron leaves it.
A sensor in the tendon: What does a Golgi tendon organ sense?
Listen for where the tendon organ sits, in series at the junction of muscle and tendon, and that it senses tension rather than stretch.
Lifting a heavier load: What does the Golgi tendon organ do to its own muscle?
Listen for the inhibitory interneuron and the muscle being told to relax as tension rises.
Stepping on a tack: How do the withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes work?
Listen for the pain signal entering the cord and spreading to interneurons on both sides.
The right leg: How do the withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes work?
Listen for which muscles contract and which relax in the leg that stepped on the tack.
The left leg: How do the withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes work?
Listen for the signal crossing the cord and the other leg straightening to take the weight.
A sensor inside the muscle: How does a muscle spindle detect stretch?
Listen for where spindles sit in the muscle and what makes their sensory neurons fire.
Stretch the muscle: How does the stretch reflex work?
Listen for the spindle afferent synapsing directly on the motor neuron to the same muscle.
Upper or lower motor neuron: What do upper motor neurons do?
Listen for where upper motor neurons start and end, and how they control the lower motor neurons in the cord.
Keeping the spindle taut: How do gamma motor neurons keep the spindle working?
The video starts at 4:52, right where this part begins. Listen for the gamma motor neurons tightening the ends of the spindle while the muscle shortens, so the spindle keeps sending signals.
A tap below the knee: Listen for the five parts: receptor, sensory neuron, integrating center, motor neuron and effector.
Counting synapses: How many synapses does a reflex use?
Listen for the difference between a monosynaptic and a polysynaptic reflex.
Cutting the dorsal root: Listen for which part of the arc carries the signal into the spinal cord.
The muscle on the other side: What does the stretch reflex do?
Listen for what the stretch reflex does to the stretched muscle. This step adds what happens to the muscle on the other side of the joint.
Spindle or tendon organ: What does the Golgi tendon organ sense?
Listen for how the tendon organ differs from the muscle spindle.
Why it cannot be monosynaptic: How many synapses does a reflex use?
Listen for why a reflex with interneurons is called polysynaptic.
Without the crossed half: How many synapses does a reflex use?
Listen for how interneurons let one signal reach more than one muscle.
The brain turns reflexes up and down: What do upper motor neurons do?
Listen for how the brain's motor pathways act on the motor neurons in the spinal cord.

latinh.s: Mechanisms and Logic in Human Physiology

rf.s: Mechanisms and Logic in Human Physiology

A stimulus that does not change: Listen for receptors that stop responding to a stimulus that stays the same, and why that is useful.
Kinds of receptors: What kinds of receptors are in the skin?
Listen for the different receptors and the kind of stimulus each one responds to.
A touch receptor in the skin: What kinds of receptors are in the skin?
Listen for how a receptor in the skin turns touch into a signal.
How does a receptor turn a stimulus into a signal?
Listen for transduction: a stimulus changing the receptor's membrane potential.
Three kinds of receptor: What kinds of receptors are in the skin?
Listen for bare nerve endings and endings wrapped in a capsule.
Swapping the jobs: Listen for receptors that keep firing and receptors that stop when the stimulus stays the same.
Tuning out the radio: Listen for how a response fades when a stimulus does not change. This step adds habituation, which happens in the brain, not the receptor.
Pressing on the ending: Listen for a change in voltage whose size depends on the stimulus. A receptor potential is a graded potential.
Reaching the trigger zone: How does a graded potential reach threshold?
Listen for how a graded potential spreads, fades with distance, and fires an action potential only if it is above threshold at the trigger zone.
Pressing on a closed eye: What is the labeled line principle?
Listen for why the brain reads the kind of stimulus from which pathway is active, not from the signal itself.
Location and the brain's map: What is the labeled line principle?
Listen for how each pathway ends in its own place in the cortex.
Two points on the skin: Listen for why small receptive fields let you tell two points apart.
Sharpening the edges: Listen for how a strongly stimulated neuron quiets its neighbors, which sharpens the edge of a stimulus.

wx.n: How reflexes work: the reflex arc, monosynaptic and polysynaptic reflexes

Receptors in the skin: What do the receptors in the skin each sense?
Listen for Meissner, Pacinian and Merkel receptors and what each one detects.
What do Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel disks sense?
Listen for vibration versus steady pressure and texture.
Fine touch from the right hand: How do the somatosensory tracts carry touch and pain?
Listen for the dorsal column pathway and where it crosses the midline.
Pain from the right hand: How do the somatosensory tracts carry touch and pain?
Listen for the pain and temperature pathway and where it crosses the midline.
Moving the right hand: What do upper motor neurons do?
Listen for the corticospinal tract running from the motor cortex to motor neurons in the cord.
The map in the cortex: Listen for why some body parts get much more cortex than others.
Hot and cold: How do we sense pain and temperature?
Listen for the receptors for warm, cold and pain, and how they differ.
Two waves of pain: How do we sense pain and temperature?
Listen for the fibers that carry pain and how fast each one is.
Gray matter and white matter: What does a spinal cord cross section show?
Listen for gray matter in the middle and white matter around it.
Horns, roots, tracts and columns: What does a spinal cord cross section show?
Listen for the posterior and anterior horns and the columns of white matter.
Cutting half the cord: What happens when half the spinal cord is cut?
Listen for which losses are on the same side and which are on the opposite side, and why.
The body's own painkillers: How does the brain turn pain down?
Listen for the pathway from the periaqueductal gray down to the spinal cord that blocks pain signals.
Regions, segments and roots: What does a spinal cord cross section show?
Listen for the dorsal and ventral roots, which carry signals into and out of the cord.
Where the cell bodies are: What does a spinal cord cross section show?
Listen for the gray matter horns and the roots that carry signals in and out.
Up and down the cord: How do the somatosensory tracts carry touch and pain?
Listen for which pathways go up the cord and where each one crosses.
A clot in the medulla: How do the somatosensory tracts carry touch and pain?
Listen for which pathway has already crossed when it reaches the medulla.
Touching a hot stove: How does a withdrawal reflex work?
Listen for how a pain signal can trigger a reflex in the spinal cord without the brain.

The Weber test: What is the difference between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss?
Listen for where each kind of loss happens, before the cochlea or in the cochlea and nerve, and which ear the sound moves toward.
The Rinne test: What is the difference between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss?
Listen for air conduction versus bone conduction, and which one is louder in each kind of loss.
Sound is a pressure wave: Listen for the outer, middle and inner ear and what each part does.
Why the middle ear has bones: Listen for the eardrum and the three small bones carrying vibration to the inner ear.
Inside the cochlea: Listen for the fluid-filled chambers, the basilar membrane and the hair cells.
Bending the hair cells: Listen for how bending the hair cells turns sound into a nerve signal.
High and low pitch: How does the brain tell high pitch from low?
Listen for where along the basilar membrane high and low sounds are detected.
Salty and sour: Listen for the five basic tastes and how taste cells detect them.
Sweet, bitter and umami: Listen for the tastes that use receptors on the taste cell surface.
A smell and a memory: Listen for the olfactory receptors, the olfactory bulb, and where smell goes in the brain.
The balance organs: How does the vestibular system work?
Listen for the semicircular canals and the two otolith organs.
Turning the head: How does the vestibular system work?
Listen for endolymph moving in a canal when the head turns.
Tilting the head: How does the vestibular system work?
Listen for the otolith organs sensing tilt and straight-line movement.
Spinning, then stopping: How does the vestibular system work?
Listen for how the fluid in the semicircular canals senses turning.
When food loses its taste: How does the sense of smell work?
Listen for how smell is detected, since much of what we call taste is smell.

A light in one eye: How does the pupillary light reflex work?
Listen for the path from the optic nerve to the midbrain and back out through the oculomotor nerve, and why both pupils constrict.
Light enters the eye: What are the parts of the eye?
Listen for the path of light through the cornea, pupil, lens and onto the retina.
A rod in the dark: Listen for what keeps a rod depolarized in the dark.
Light hits rhodopsin: Listen for each step from light hitting rhodopsin to the channels closing.
Seeing a dim star: How are rods and cones different?
Listen for which works in dim light, which sees color, and where each is found.
Crossing at the chiasm: How does the brain process the visual field?
Listen for which fibers cross at the optic chiasm and which stay on the same side.
Pressure on the chiasm: How does the brain process the visual field?
Listen for what each half of the visual field sends to each side of the brain.
Releasing transmitter: What cells are in the retina?
Listen for the path from rods and cones to bipolar cells to ganglion cells.
Center and surround: What cells are in the retina?
Listen for the ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve, and the fovea.
Cutting the left optic nerve: How does the brain process the visual field?
Listen for which fibers cross at the optic chiasm and which stay on the same side.
An eye that is too long: Listen for nearsightedness and why the image focuses in front of the retina.
An eye that is too short: Listen for farsightedness and why the image focuses behind the retina.
Reading at 60: Listen for presbyopia, the stiffening of the lens with age.

Three membranes: Listen for the dura, arachnoid and pia mater, from outside in.
Taking a sample: Where is the fluid sampled in a spinal tap?
Listen for the lumbar cistern, the space below the end of the cord.
The fluid around the brain: Listen for what cerebrospinal fluid does and where it is made.
Where it is made and where it goes: Listen for the lateral, third and fourth ventricles and the cerebral aqueduct that connects them.
When the aqueduct is blocked: Listen for what happens when cerebrospinal fluid builds up, and how it is treated.
Two kinds of capillary: Listen for the tight junctions between endothelial cells and the astrocyte end-feet.
Drowsy or not: Listen for which kinds of substances can and cannot cross.
Where the barrier is missing: Listen for the circumventricular organs, the places with no barrier, and why.
Four things arrive: What does the blood-brain barrier let through?
Listen for what can cross the barrier and what is kept out.
Feeding the brain: What does the blood-brain barrier let through?
Listen for how needed nutrients get across the barrier.
